Substitution of E[Dt+1 | Ht+1 ] = Vt+1 +bt+1 into Equation (4.9) and collection of the regression
errors proves the identity. The first line is a local product of nuisance errors; the second
transports all later error backward. Very large early ratios can amplify an otherwise modest
continuation error. A small one-step prediction loss is therefore an inadequate diagnostic for a
long-horizon causal value estimator.


4.9     Learning the continuation rather than the whole trajectory
Forward simulation of the g-formula needs a conditional distribution for every covariate
whose future realization affects decisions or rewards. For a large mixed record of balances,
transactions, arrears and categorical eligibility, building a coherent joint transition can be
difficult. Recursive regression instead learns only the conditional continuation needed for a
fixed policy and outcome. It can be much cheaper when the target is narrow. The price is
that a different policy, horizon or outcome can require a new sequence of regressions.
  A simulation model is more reusable for new policy scenarios but exposes more mechanisms to
misspecification. A reward model, balance evolution, observation process and action eligibility
must evolve together. Simulating arrears independently of credit limits can generate impossible
account states. Neural g-computation offers flexible conditional laws (Li et al., 2020); flexibility
does not remove the obligation to preserve account identities and interventions. The product
should compare simulated policy values with recursive estimates when both are identified, not
judge the simulator only by factual one-step prediction.
  For either approach, partition complete customer or household histories before training.
Within each training fold, generate future pseudo-outcomes without using the held-out cus-
tomer’s outcomes. A naive implementation can cross-fit the last regression while leaking the
held-out outcome through an earlier fitted continuation. The complete dependency graph of
nuisance fits must respect the fold boundary. Nested and longitudinal orthogonal methods
4.10. Targeted estimation and bounded outcomes                                               25


formalize rate and error-control requirements for such constructions (Chernozhukov et al.,
2022b; Singh, 2022).
   This distinction also affects hyperparameter tuning. Tuning on final policy value can adapt
to noise in the evaluation trajectories. Prediction-based tuning within training folds preserves
the declared evaluation, though it may not minimize policy-value error. An outer evaluation
of the entire training and selection procedure is needed when the scientific claim is about that
procedure rather than one frozen policy.


4.10     Targeted estimation and bounded outcomes
For a binary terminal event, a fitted conditional probability should remain between zero and
                                                   b 0 and a one-dimensional parameter ϵ:
one. A simple logistic fluctuation uses an initial Q t

                                                    b 0 + ϵH ∗ ,
                                        b ϵ = logit Q
                                  logit Q t           t     t

where the chosen covariate Ht∗ or equivalent observation weight is constructed from the
treatment and censoring mechanism for the target. Fitting the fluctuation so the relevant
weighted residual is zero aligns the plug-in estimate with an influence-function equation. A
longitudinal procedure updates backward through the continuation regressions.
   The displayed expression describes the mechanism, not a complete universal TMLE algorithm.
Different targets require different clever covariates, weight conventions and recursion. The
implementation must state whether outcomes have been bounded or rescaled, what happens
at fitted probabilities zero and one, and how targeting convergence is checked. The relevant
sequential robustness analysis is estimator-specific (Luedtke et al., 2018). This is why a
longitudinal adapter should retain its native algorithm and diagnostics instead of wrapping
every estimator behind a function that returns only a scalar “effect.”
   Targeting can respect the parameter space while a one-step correction falls outside it in a
small sample. That is a useful finite-sample feature, but does not repair practical positivity
or unmeasured confounding. Conversely, an out-of-range one-step estimate is a diagnostic of
instability; silently clipping it to a probability conceals the issue and changes inference.


4.11     Observation loss has its own clock and model
Let Ct+1 = 1 mean the next required record remains observed, conditional on being observed
through t. Write its conditional probability as ct (Ht , At ). If observation is conditionally
independent of the relevant future potential outcomes given that information, a change-of-
measure weight contains
                                       t
                                         gs (As | Hs )     Cs+1
                             Wtg,C =
                                       Y
                                                                     .
                                          e (As | Hs ) cs (Hs , As )
                                       s=0 s

This formula separates two missing pieces: the action law and the reporting law. Exact
randomized treatment probabilities do not make a selectively missing outcome ignorable. A
customer whose debt is sold may have an observed sale price, an unobserved later recovery
and a changed economic owner. The appropriate bank contribution can be observed at sale
even though a different lifetime recovery outcome is censored.
  Administrative censoring at a fixed cutoff also changes maturity. A recent cohort may have
complete six-month outcomes but no twelve-month outcomes. A twelve-month effect then
needs older cohorts, a shorter target or an extrapolation model. More recent transactions
26                                                              Causal analysis for a universal bank


cannot fill calendar time that has not elapsed. The data contract stores both the outcome end
date and the date by which the outcome could actually be known.
   Competing events need the same discipline. Prepayment is not an arbitrary missing default
label. It changes the bank’s remaining claim and may itself be affected by assistance or pricing.
Estimating default cumulative incidence, event-free survival, a hypothetical no-prepayment
risk and discounted bank contribution are four different questions. Equation (4.8) answers the
first under a regime; the cash-flow recursion can answer the fourth without pretending that
prepayment never occurs.


4.12      Structural blips and dynamic effect parameters
Sometimes the bank wants an interpretable effect parameter rather than a complete regime
value. Consider a two-action additive model in which the conditional causal contribution of the
final action is ψ1 A1 . Removing this contribution creates a blipped outcome Y blip = Y − ψ1 A1 .
A g-estimation moment compares that outcome across earlier actions after conditioning on
their histories. With an appropriate structural nested model, one estimates the final blip first
and moves backward, avoiding ordinary conditioning that blocks the earlier mediated effect.
   Dynamic DML combines this recursive removal with orthogonal nuisance residualization
(Lewis and Syrgkanis, 2021). The gains are a compact effect parameterization and flexible
adjustment; the costs are the restrictions of the structural model, the need for support
and dependence-compatible sampling. Constant blips, heterogeneous blips and arbitrary
dynamic regimes are different model classes. The bank should choose among them according
to the decision and interpretability requirement rather than the apparent modernity of the
implementation.
   The recommended comparison therefore has three tiers. An interpretable structured model
estimates a small set of economically meaningful dynamic effects. Recursive DR or targeted
estimation evaluates a prespecified set of feasible regimes. A flexible transition or representation
model explores where those simpler constructions miss important history. Agreement is useful
evidence under shared assumptions; disagreement is a reason to inspect targets, support and
model restrictions, not to average incompatible answers.
Chapter 5

Time series, dependence and
computational scale

5.1    Three different large-data regimes

A bank may observe millions of short customer histories, a smaller panel of branches exposed
to common shocks, or one long aggregate balance-sheet series. These regimes have different
asymptotics and different independent information. Pooling them into one large table does
not make them independent.
  For a stationary scalar score series with summable autocovariances, the variance of its
average is approximately
                                                          
                                 1             X          
                   Var(ϕ̄T ) ≃         γ0 + 2         γk       ,   γk = Cov(ϕt , ϕt−k ).   (5.1)
                                 T             k≥1
                                                           


For an AR(1)-like correlation pattern, the variance-based illustrative effective sample size is
T (1 − ρ)/(1 + ρ). At ρ = 0.9, it is about T /19. This calculation concerns a stationary mean;
it is not a general causal-information measure for nonstationary bank data.


5.2    A fold is an information boundary

Customer-level cross-fitting keeps the complete customer’s trajectory outside its nuisance-
training fold. Household or connected-business interference can require a larger unit. A
prospective evaluation also uses training data available before its evaluation origin, with
embargoes covering feature lookback and overlapping outcome windows where needed.
   Retrospective estimation under a justified stationary sampling design may use different folds
from a prospective deployment simulation. The product must distinguish the two. Randomly
splitting account-month rows leaks individual histories. Pure time splitting can still share a
common economic shock between training and test entities. There is no universal split that
repairs every dependence structure.
   Multiway-cluster DML splits along cluster dimensions under a specific sampling framework
(Chiang et al., 2021). For crossed clustering, a familiar score covariance construction adds
cluster contributions and subtracts their intersection, schematically

                                 Vb = Vbentity + Vbdate − Vbentity,date .

                                                      27
28                                                               Causal analysis for a universal bank


Scaling and finite-sample corrections depend on the estimator. Few clusters, unbalanced groups
and indefinite finite-sample estimates require disclosure and suitable alternatives. Increasing
the number of accounts cannot replace missing independent policy dates.
   HAC estimators, block bootstraps and cluster bootstraps must match the score process
and dependence assumptions. The report records bandwidth/block length, cluster counts,
sensitivity and any finite-sample correction. Generic package defaults are not a scientific
inference specification.


5.3     Changing regimes and transport
Rates, underwriting policies and customer behavior change. A pooled coefficient across pre-
pandemic, crisis and high-rate periods may have little decision relevance. Stability diagnostics
should examine treatment policy, covariate support, residual distributions and effect hetero-
geneity by regime. Change-point detection is evidence of distributional change, not a unique
explanation for it.
   Transporting a conditional effect from source S = 1 to target S = 0 may use E[τ (X) | S = 0]
if the relevant conditional response is invariant and target covariates have source support.
The target distribution must be recorded. Unobserved effect modifiers, product versions
and changes in interference can invalidate transport even when feature distributions overlap.
Banking macro and equilibrium responses can change the mechanism itself (Beraja et al., 2019;
Benetton, 2021).


5.4     Interference and shared constraints
Customers can share households, firms can share owners, and offers can compete for branch
capacity. In such settings write Yi (ai , zi ), where zi = fi (a−i , G) summarizes others’ assignments
through a declared network G. The exposure mapping is a substantive restriction: it asserts
which features of others’ treatment matter. Individual potential outcomes indexed only by ai
are inadequate under interference (Hernán and Robins, 2020).
   Direct effects compare Yi (1, z)−Yi (0, z) at fixed exposure; spillover effects compare exposures
at fixed own action. A group policy effect changes both. Household or branch randomization,
or randomized treatment saturation across groups, can create the relevant variation when
operationally appropriate. Independent-unit inference must then use the randomized or
plausibly independent groups.
  For observational networks, homophily, endogenous links and unobserved shared shocks
complicate identification. Neither a graph database nor clustered standard errors eliminates
these problems. The initial product should support declared partial-interference groups and
report when cross-group spillovers remain plausible. General network identification is a research
extension, not a promised default feature.


5.5     Compute around scientific boundaries
The execution engine should materialize a versioned eligible population, partition by the
independent unit, compute fold-specific nuisances, and aggregate scores with the declared
cluster keys. Map tasks may fit independent folds or bootstrap replicates; reductions retain
sufficient statistics and covariance blocks. Every retry uses the same input snapshot and
random seed. Hyperparameter search occurs inside nuisance-training partitions.
5.6. A measurable scale qualification                                                         29


   Dense data footprints are already material. At 108 rows and 256 float32 features, the feature
array alone is 102.4 GB in decimal units, before identifiers, outcomes, fold indicators, copies
and model state. Use columnar projection, predicate pushdown, partition pruning, streamed
score evaluation and sparse representations when justified. Avoid materializing all lagged
columns and all horizons for every exploratory study.
   Finite-state filtering costs O(N T K 2 ) for dense K-state transitions, or less with sparse
structure. The forward pass needs O(K) working state per active sequence; storing all
smoothing messages costs O(T K) per sequence unless checkpointing/recomputation is used.
State dimension, not just row count, can dominate. Particle methods trade computation for
approximation variance and degeneracy diagnostics.
   Temporal graph search can be more difficult still. A coarse p2 L candidate count already gives
three million directed lag candidates for p = 500, L = 12, before conditioning-set search. Apply
justified temporal and domain constraints, variable grouping and staged screening. Screening
can discard true parents and must be evaluated as part of the discovery procedure. Distributed
execution does not eliminate the statistical multiple-testing or combinatorial problem.


5.6     A measurable scale qualification
The benchmark program should use three tiers: 105 rows for correctness, 107 for multi-team
workflows, and 108 for large group studies. These are future test sizes, not achieved performance
claims. Benchmark fixed estimands and equivalent estimators on single-node and distributed
execution. Measure peak memory, wall time, compute cost, serialization, retry behavior and
numerical agreement. Report nuisance-fitting and data-preparation costs separately.
   Use an explicitly documented reference machine before stating latency targets. A candidate
target is interactive cohort diagnostics within 30 seconds on a precomputed study snapshot and
scheduled large-study completion within one working day. These are design goals contingent
on workload and hardware. They must not be advertised as measured service levels. Scientific
stopping rules take precedence: a fast job with unsupported actions or invalid uncertainty has
not completed an acceptable study.


5.7     Dynamic responses: local projections and structural VARs
A treasury question often concerns a path: how does a funding shock today change deposits,
lending and contribution over the next twelve months? Write a stable reduced-form VAR as
                             L
                                                                 E[εt ε′t ] = I.
                             X
                      Xt =         Aℓ Xt−ℓ + ut ,   ut = Cεt ,                              (5.2)
                             ℓ=1

The lag coefficients describe conditional dynamics. The structural impact matrix C maps
economically interpretable shocks to reduced-form innovations. Estimating Aℓ and Σu = CC ′
does not in general identify C. For any orthogonal Q, (CQ)(CQ)′ = Σu . An identifying
restriction must choose among observationally compatible shock decompositions or return a
set of responses.
   For a VAR(1), the response at horizon h to shock j is Ah Cej . A recursive timing restriction
selects a triangular factor of Σu . Its interpretation is a statement about which variables can
respond contemporaneously. Ordering funding before lending may be plausible at one frequency
and implausible at another. The selected order must be attached to the impulse-response
report as an assumption, not hidden in a default Cholesky routine.
30                                                            Causal analysis for a universal bank


     Local projections estimate each horizon directly, for example
                                                              (h)
                               Yt+h = αh + βh Dt + Γ′h Wt + vt+h ,                            (5.3)

where Dt is the shock or endogenous intervention variable and Wt contains the declared controls.
Without an identification argument, βh is a projection coefficient. When Dt represents a
suitably identified shock, it can estimate a dynamic causal response. Direct horizon estimation
permits flexible responses and avoids imposing all finite-order VAR restrictions, often with a
variance cost. The review by Jordà and Taylor (2024) explains both the connection and the
finite-sample tradeoffs; it does not justify a universal preference for one method.


5.7.1      External instruments identify a particular shock

An external instrument Zt must correlate with the shock of interest and be orthogonal to
the other shocks that enter the dynamic outcome. Under the moving-average representation
Xt = h≥0 Θh εt−h , assume E[Zt ε1t ] = α ̸= 0 and E[Zt εj,t+k ] = 0 for other contemporaneous
      P

shocks and for the relevant nonzero leads and lags. Normalize the impact of shock one on X1t
to unity. Then
                                             E[Zt Xi,t+h ]
                                     Θh,i1 =               .                             (5.4)
                                              E[Zt X1t ]
The numerator equals αΘh,i1 because all other shock covariances vanish; the denominator
equals α under the normalization. This is the dynamic covariance-ratio argument in Stock
and Watson (2018, Section 2.3). Controls require the corresponding partialled-out restrictions.
   The lead-lag exclusion is substantive. A monetary-policy announcement surprise might also
reveal information about future economic conditions. A bank funding instrument may reflect
a local demand shock. A strong first stage does not exclude either channel. Direct LP-IV and
a proxy SVAR have different information requirements: the latter normally needs a suitable
invertibility or recoverability argument, while the direct approach in the stated source can
avoid invertibility under stronger lead-lag exclusions. The product must retain that distinction
when offering both estimators.
   An intervention that raises a bank’s posted rate for three months is also different from
a one-time structural shock with endogenous future rate responses. An impulse response
describes the latter under a maintained system. A sustained policy path requires a different
intervention or structural policy simulation. Calling both a “25-basis-point scenario” would
conceal an economically material difference.

5.9. A repeated-sample demonstration of common shocks                                         31


Bandwidth b, kernel, centering, finite-sample adjustment and the range of available T determine
the approximation. Short series and persistent scores can yield poor finite-sample coverage
even with a familiar HAC label.
   Overlapping horizons make the distinction useful. In an AR(1), repeated substitution gives
Xt+h = ρh Xt + hj=1 ρh−j ut+j . The projection residuals overlap and are serially correlated.
                P

Some lag-augmented local-projection constructions make the relevant score serially uncorrelated
under stronger innovation conditions, allowing heteroskedasticity-robust inference. That
conclusion comes from the regressor–innovation structure, not from denying residual overlap.
Jordà and Taylor (2024, Section 6) distinguishes these cases. Its reviewed uniform-inference
result should not be transferred without proof to arbitrary multiway bank panels or learned
nonlinear nuisance scores.
   Pointwise intervals for twelve horizons also do not give a simultaneous 95% band for the
response path. A maximum-statistic bootstrap, a justified joint Gaussian approximation or a
conservative multiplicity adjustment can answer the pathwise question. The resampling must
preserve the time and cluster structure. A funding decision depending on the discounted sum
of the response needs the covariance across horizons, which can be much more informative
than reading individual significance stars.



5.9     A repeated-sample demonstration of common shocks

The supplied experiment draws a score panel

                    ϕit = ai + ft + ϵit ,     ai , ft , ϵit independent N (0, 1),

with 96 entities and 36 dates. The target mean is zero. Direct variance calculation yields

                                              1   1   1
                                  Var(ϕ̄) =     +   +       .                               (5.5)
                                              96 36 96 · 36

The resulting true standard error is approximately 0.1962. There are 3,456 rows, but shared
entity and date shocks dominate the uncertainty. Treating rows as independent counts those
shocks repeatedly.

                        Variance method            Mean SE 95% coverage
                        Rows independent              0.029            0.227
                        Entity clusters               0.103            0.693

Table 5.1: Coverage over 1,200 independently generated panels. Critical values are normal; the
crossed construction uses entity and date corrections. This is a stated Gaussian score design,
not a theorem for arbitrary bank panels.

  Entity clustering protects against repeated observations of a customer but misses the date
component in this design. The crossed construction is much closer to the intended coverage,
while only 36 date clusters still make finite-sample approximation relevant. The code retains the
Monte Carlo standard error of every reported coverage estimate. Adding a million customers
would reduce the first and third terms in Equation (5.5); it would leave the date term. This is
why the execution planner must preserve the scientific unit rather than simply distribute all
rows uniformly over workers.

5.10                                     Large scale has several different bottlenecks

The scientific workload can be decomposed as



                                             Tjob = Tsnapshot + Tdesign + Tnuisance + Tscore + Tinference + Texport ,



with separate memory and storage accounts. A fast score reduction can be irrelevant when
source reconstruction or repeated nuisance fitting dominates. Likewise, a GPU can accelerate
dense model fitting while increasing the cost of copying sparse event data into device memory.
The product should measure each stage and retain the workload configuration with the result.
   Consider N independent trajectories, horizon T , K latent states, p observed variables, L
candidate lags, F folds and B bootstrap replicates. These dimensions describe different jobs.
Dense HMM smoothing requires order N T K 2 arithmetic per likelihood pass. Refitting all
parameters in every bootstrap can multiply that work by B, not merely add a cheap variance
reduction. A temporal graph learner may have p2 L candidate edges and far more conditioning
tests. A flexible longitudinal nuisance pipeline may fit a distinct learner for each date, fold
and target policy. Reporting only total rows misses each of these sources of difficulty.
   Several computational reductions have scientific conditions. Homogeneous transition counts
can be summed across customers only when the same parameterization applies. State com-
pression must preserve the decision- relevant conditional law. Pooling across jurisdictions
can improve precision only under a defensible sharing or hierarchical model. Sparse graph
screening reduces search only by making a restriction on candidate parents. Each reduction
belongs in the model specification and sensitivity study.
   The recommended architecture caches reusable source snapshots and fold-consistent nuisance
predictions, streams score evaluation, and reduces cluster contributions without materializing
unnecessary dense copies. It parallelizes independent fits or sequences before splitting a
dependent sequence. For long-sequence smoothing, checkpointing trades recomputation for
storage; truncating a sequence instead changes the conditional information available to the
estimator. Those are different operations.
5.11. A scale result must preserve the statistical result                                    33


5.11      A scale result must preserve the statistical result
The construction chapter supplies a measured streaming reduction workload and a temporal-
revision implementation. These bounded measurements establish the operation and resource
use of those components. They do not establish end-to-end performance for a causal forest,
temporal graph search or controlled-state likelihood on a banking group’s records.
   A future large-scale qualification uses identical source snapshots, folds, target weights and
random seeds for a single-node reference and a distributed implementation. It compares
estimates, influence contributions, covariance, unsupported-cell flags and financial totals, not
just runtime. Differences caused by floating-point summation are bounded; differences caused
by changed folds or dropped records are scientific defects. Retry tests must show that a failed
worker does not duplicate a customer’s contribution.
   Resource budgets should be expressed per workload: bytes scanned per study, peak worker
memory, total CPU/GPU time, shuffled bytes, model checkpoints, and the number of complete
refits. A claim such as “supports one hundred million rows” becomes useful only after specifying
these quantities, the estimator and the attainable uncertainty. Computation can make a valid
analysis feasible; it cannot create additional independent policy shocks.
Chapter 6

Partial observation, estimation and
policy value

6.1     A precise event clock

Repeated bank decisions may depend on unobserved financial resilience, liquidity needs or
customer intent. A POMDP represents a latent state St , an observation Ot available before
action At , a reward Rt , and the next state and observation. Let Ht = (O0 , A0 , R0 , . . . , Ot )
be the recorded decision history. The policy available to the bank must be measurable with
respect to this history, or to an explicitly enlarged logged information set.
   For clarity, suppose a finite-state model has initial law µθ , initial emission Bθ (o0 | s0 ),
transition Pθ (s′ | s, a), reward density Fθ (r | s, a, s′ ) and next emission Bθ (o′ | s′ , a). These
factorization choices are modeling assumptions. A joint emission for rewards and signals may
be needed when conditional independence is inappropriate.
   Let the behavior policy be qη (a | s, h), potentially using private information summarized by
s. The observed-data likelihood for one trajectory is
                  X
      L(θ, η) =          µθ (s0 )Bθ (o0 | s0 )
                  s0:T
                   −1
                  TY
              ×          qη (at | st , ht )Pθ (st+1 | st , at )Fθ (rt | st , at , st+1 )Bθ (ot+1 | st+1 , at ).   (6.1)
                  t=0


Omitting the behavior factor is justified for estimating environment parameters when action
assignment depends only on the recorded history and is parameter-distinct: it can then be
factored out of the latent-state sum in the joint likelihood. If the logger uses unobserved
information, the action itself is evidence about latent state and the factor cannot generally
be removed. Fitting a model conditional on the action sequence without this distinction can
misinterpret selection as a transition effect.



6.2     Filtering, smoothing and estimation

The belief-state construction connects partial observation to planning (Kaelbling et al., 1998);
estimation additionally requires an explicit likelihood. For an observed-history policy, after
observing Ot and previous rewards, let bt (s) = Pθ (St = s | Ht ). The action is not an additional

  Normalizers from the forward recursion accumulate the log likelihood, avoiding numerical
underflow. Backward messages produce smoothed state probabilities and expected transition
counts. In an EM algorithm,
                                                 P                    ′

updates tabular transitions, with explicit prior/regularization when counts are small. Emission
and reward parameters are updated consistently with their likelihood. Unobserved-logger
parameters, if included, require their own model and identification restrictions.
   Alternatives include direct differentiation of the marginalized likelihood, Bayesian inference,
variational approximations and particle methods for nonlinear continuous states. Compare
multiple initializations, held-out predictive likelihood, residual dynamics, posterior predictive
checks, parameter recovery and prior sensitivity. Label permutations require a normalization
or permutation-invariant comparison. Numerical convergence and good predictive fit do not
establish causal identification.



6.3     Statistical and causal identification differ

Alexandrovich et al. (2016) establish HMM identification under full-rank ergodic transitions,
distinct emissions and other stated conditions, up to state labels. This is a result about an
observed distribution within an HMM class. A controlled bank model additionally needs
sufficiently informative actions, identifiable reward/observation mechanisms and an intervention
interpretation. The stationary uncontrolled theorem does not supply all of these conditions.

Proposition 6.1 (Observed fit need not identify an action effect). There exist two binary-
action binary-outcome models with the same strictly positive observed law and different average
treatment effects.


Proof. In model I, U ∼ Bernoulli(1/2), P(A = 1 | U ) = 0.2 + 0.6U and P(Y = 1 | U, A) =
0.2 + 0.6U . Action has no causal effect. In model II, A ∼ Bernoulli(1/2) independently and
P(Y = 1 | A) = 0.32 + 0.36A. Its effect is 0.36. Both imply P(A, Y ) = (0.34, 0.16, 0.16, 0.34) in
cell order (0, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (1, 1). Their observational likelihoods agree while their intervention
distributions differ.


   This one-step counterexample embeds in a sequential problem. Observed action positivity
and perfect predictive fit therefore cannot guarantee causal policy identification. The practical
remedy is an explicit route: randomized or measured-history assignment, defensible structural
restrictions, valid instruments/proxies, or partial identification.
36                                                                  Causal analysis for a universal bank


6.4     Proxies and instruments are measurement designs

In a static proximal model let U be hidden confounding, Z a treatment-inducing proxy, W an
outcome-inducing proxy and X observed covariates. One bridge equation is

                            E[Y | Z, A, X] = E[h(W, A, X) | Z, A, X].                              (6.3)

Under latent exchangeability, proxy exclusions such as Y ⊥ Z | A, U, X and W ⊥ (A, Z) | U, X,
completeness, bridge existence and support, a causal mean can be expressed as E[h(W, a, X)]
(Miao et al., 2018; Tchetgen Tchetgen et al., 2020). The exclusions describe how variables are
generated. Two highly predictive features are not necessarily two valid proxies.
   The bridge is an inverse problem. Weak proxies can make it ill-conditioned; regularization
trades variance against bias. Minimax methods and regression bridges provide estimation
strategies under corresponding restrictions (Ghassami et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2024). The
product should show proxy-role justification, bridge residuals, conditioning diagnostics and
regularization sensitivity; these do not empirically prove completeness.
  POMDP/proximal OPE theories impose particular information and proxy structures (Ten-
nenholtz et al., 2020; Bennett et al., 2021; Bennett and Kallus, 2023). IV-based sequential
evaluation also requires relevance, exclusion, interaction restrictions and dynamic conditional
independences (Xu et al., 2023). These are research-grade options for a bank with the right
measurement design, not generic repairs for absent action logs. Recent hidden-treatment
work similarly requires informative surrogates and additional proxy restrictions (Zhou and
Tchetgen Tchetgen, 2026).


6.5     Policy evaluation before optimization

The actor must also be clear. A POMDP policy can describe a bank choosing actions given
customer-state uncertainty. A customer’s refinancing or account-closing choice is a different
behavior model, potentially with private preferences, switching costs and beliefs. Estimating
that choice model requires restrictions on utility, expectations and state transitions. Optimizing
the bank’s supplied reward function does not identify customer preferences. Structural demand
or dynamic choice components can supply this behavior only with their own identifying
evidence.
  With sufficient observed histories and unconfounded logging, a target policy π has finite-
horizon value

   A separate simulation generates 700 trajectories of 14 randomized actions. With
emissions and initial law fixed and known, likelihood optimization recovers the four
transition-to-fragile probabilities as approximately (0.0935, 0.7002, 0.0774, 0.4192) against
truth (0.1, 0.75, 0.05, 0.45). Three starts converge to closely agreeing objectives; maximum
absolute error is 0.050. This verifies a small controlled estimation construction. It does not
establish unknown-emission identification, uncertainty coverage, real-bank state recovery or
bank policy value.
  Counterfactual trajectories introduce another distinction. A Gumbel-max structural model
specifies an exogenous-noise coupling across actions (Oberst and Sontag, 2019). Different
couplings can share transition probabilities while producing different individual counterfactual
paths. The product should label such paths as model-conditional scenarios.
Chapter 7

Constructing a controlled
latent-state estimator

7.1     The estimation problem the product must own
A planning library generally expects transition, observation and reward models. A bank
has transactions, incomplete measurements and a historical decision process. Bridging those
objects is a substantive product capability. The estimation module must specify a latent-state
model, reconstruct its event clock, fit the observed-data likelihood, quantify uncertainty and
state the conditions under which changing the action mechanism has a causal interpretation.
Passing a fitted transition matrix to a POMDP solver leaves most of that work unresolved.
   For K states, M signal categories and a finite action set, the model has K − 1 + |A|K(K −
1) + K(M − 1) free probabilities before reward, covariate and logging parameters. Small K
makes exact marginalization possible and is appropriate for a first implementation. Increasing
K creates flexibility, weakly separated states and more local optima; state count is a model-
selection question, not a quality score. A state name such as “fragile liquidity” is an economic
hypothesis. Ordering states by expected delinquency fixes a label convention; it does not
establish a unique financial mechanism.


7.2     Forward and backward messages
Suppress a separate reward emission and define the observed transition kernel
                      Mt (s, s′ ) = qη (at | s, ht )Pθ (s′ | s, at )Bθ (ot+1 | s′ , at ).
When logging uses only observed history and its parameters are distinct, its factor is constant
across latent paths and can be omitted from the objective for environment parameters. This is
a joint-likelihood factorization argument. It does not assert that adaptively chosen actions are
independent of observations, or that the remaining factor is the ordinary conditional density
of observations given the entire future action sequence.
  Let αt be the normalized filter after the current signal and preceding observations and
actions. Start with c0 = s µ(s)B(o0 | s) and α0 (s) = µ(s)B(o0 | s)/c0 . Then

They extend the expected-count construction described by Rabiner (1989, pp.264–266) to the

additional state information.
   The distinction between filtering and smoothing matters operationally. Filtering uses
information available at the decision. Smoothing uses later observations and actions to revise
the historical state estimate. A plot of smoothed fragility may help diagnose a fitted model,
but using that series as a feature in a retrospective “prospective” policy evaluation would leak
future information.


7.3     The M step is a constrained count calculation
The expected complete log likelihood contains
                                                         ′
         X                   X                                  X                         X
                                       P                               B                          q
              Ns0 log µs +            Nass ′ log Pa (s, s ) +         Nso log Bs (o) +           Nsa log qs (a).
          s                  a,s,s′                             s,o                        s,a

The counts sum γ and ξ over trajectories with the appropriate observed action or signal.
                                               P                       P
A Lagrange multiplier shows that maximizing j Nj log pj subject to j pj = 1 gives pj =
    P
Nj / k Nk . Row-wise application updates the initial law, transitions, emissions and, when
modeled, logging probabilities. Structural zeros must follow from the model; small positive
pseudocounts are disclosed regularization.
   The E step allocates each trajectory probabilistically among states. The M step updates
the specified likelihood from those expected counts. A Viterbi path instead chooses a single
most probable state sequence. Treating that path as observed data discards state uncertainty
and generally does not maximize the same likelihood. A convenient visualization must not
silently replace the estimator.
  EM need not reach a global maximum. Multiple starts, likelihood increments, iteration caps,
boundary probabilities and state separation belong in the fit receipt. Direct differentiation of
the scaled marginalized likelihood is a useful challenger. Bayesian inference adds priors and
posterior computation; variational estimation introduces approximation error. None supplies
causal identification through numerical convergence.


7.4     Unknown emissions and hidden logging: a fitted study
The study generates 800 independent trajectories with twelve actions, two latent states and
three signal categories:
                                                    !                         !                                    !
                                         .93 .07                      .94 .06                    .78 .18 .04
      µ = (.72, .28),        P0 =                ,         P1 =               ,       B=                     .
                                         .22 .78                      .52 .48                    .16 .34 .50

The learner receives only signals and actions. Four starts estimate the initial law, transitions
and emissions; labels are aligned by expected signal severity before parameter errors are
evaluated. The generator’s latent states never enter estimation.
40                                                                    Causal analysis for a universal bank


   Randomized logging chooses action one with probability 0.4. In the observational design its
probabilities are 0.15 and 0.80 in the two hidden states. The same observational trajectories
are fitted with and without a state-dependent logging factor. The joint fit estimates that
factor as well. The experiment stipulates the finite model and invariance of transitions and
observations under an action intervention. Those restrictions make the generated environment
causal; the estimation code does not discover their truth.

        Estimation design                     Max P error Max B error Policy gain (USD)
        Randomized                                    0.026            0.054                24.90
        Hidden logging, omitted action law            0.384            0.066               -22.40
        Hidden logging, joint action law              0.045            0.007                13.61

Table 7.1: Unknown-emission estimation. The policy contrast is assistance after the most
severe current signal versus no assistance, over eight decisions. The true gain is USD 22.34.

   The omitted-action model reverses the sign of the policy contrast in this sample. Historical
assistance reveals fragility; ignoring that selection can interpret a selected post-assistance
distribution as a harmful action effect. The joint model corrects this particular mechanism,
but its single-sample value remains materially different from truth. Raw objective values from
the two fitting routes are not directly comparable because the joint objective includes the
action density.

                 Action model Gain bias (USD) Gain RMSE Transition RMSE
                 Omitted                     -38.95           39.08               0.203
                 Joint                         3.41           21.90               0.051

Table 7.2: Thirty independently generated observational datasets of 500 trajectories, with
both fitting routes applied to each dataset. Correct logging specification improves parameter
recovery but leaves substantial policy-value variability.

   The omitted model’s mean policy-gain error is approximately USD −38.95, with Monte Carlo
standard error USD 0.59. The joint model’s mean error is USD 3.41 with Monte Carlo standard
error USD 4.02, and RMSE USD 21.90. These results expose a failure and a conditional
remedy. They do not show that every controlled hidden-state model is identified or that the
remaining uncertainty permits a bank decision. The runs retain finite iteration budgets. All
30 selected omitted-action fits and seven of the 30 joint fits hit the 120-iteration repetition
cap. The repeated table therefore compares the implemented finite-budget procedures, not
fully optimized population estimators. Its error contains optimization as well as sampling and
specification effects.
   A separate same-data convergence check extends the main observational fits to a maximum
of 2,000 iterations without changing data or starting seeds. The omitted-action fit meets the
stopping criterion at 163 iterations for its best start and still gives a policy gain near negative
USD 22.40; the joint fit again gives positive USD 13.61. Thus the main sign reversal persists
after the stated numerical stopping test. This does not establish a global optimum or isolate
all specification bias in the repeated study.


7.5     Uncertainty includes the observation model
Seventy-nine trajectory bootstrap resamples of the randomized dataset refit initial probabilities,
transitions and emissions, holding the two policies fixed. The percentile interval for their
7.6. Planning with a distribution over states                                                      41


value difference is approximately USD [14.61, 38.91]. The bootstrap count gives coarse tail
quantiles; one selected bootstrap fit hits its 120-iteration cap. This is a model-conditional
interval for independent trajectories, not a coverage study or an interval for unrestricted hidden
confounding in bank records.
   Additional uncertainty arises from the state specification, intervention invariance and policy
selection. A bootstrap holding those choices fixed does not address them. A fitted three-state
model may describe historical observations as well as a two-state model and value an untested
policy differently. An assistance action may alter reporting intensity as well as liquidity. A
policy selected from hundreds of candidates may exploit noise. Each requires a separate
comparison, sensitivity analysis or outer evaluation design.
   The product should show state separation, transition support, likelihood profiles or posterior
dependence, predictive residuals by regime, and financial decision sensitivity. A large parameter
interval need not imply a large value interval, and a small parameter error can reverse a close
policy comparison. The decision determines which uncertainty matters.


7.6     Planning with a distribution over states
For a correctly specified environment and an actor restricted to recorded history, let b be
its state belief, p(o′ | b, a) the next-signal law and τ (b, a, o′ ) its Bayes update. With feasible
actions A(b) and expected reward r(b, a),
                                     "                                                     #
                                                            p(o′ | b, a)Vt+1 {τ (b, a, o′ )} .
                                                       X
                   Vt (b) = max          r(b, a) + γ                                             (7.4)
                            a∈A(b)
                                                       o′

Observed eligibility must be part of the information state if it changes the action set. The
continuation averages future state uncertainty and future information. A myopic threshold
neglects both continuation rewards and any value of information (Kaelbling et al., 1998).
   The study values next-signal contribution at (18, 0, −90) dollars and charges eight dollars
for assistance. Reward is a deterministic function of the next signal and action, so no separate
reward information is omitted from the filter. A 501-point belief grid solves eight-decision
control. Doubling resolution changes initial value by less than USD 0.0001. Under the supplied
true model, values are approximately −21.92 for no assistance, 0.42 for assistance after a
severe signal, and 5.30 for the grid policy. These numerical comparisons do not show that the
extra optimized value is statistically resolved by the fitted data.
  For bounded rewards and γ < 1, the infinite-horizon Bellman operator is a contraction of
modulus γ: expectation changes by at most the supremum change in continuation; discounting
multiplies the bound by γ; taking a maximum preserves it. This establishes a unique fixed
point for the supplied belief-MDP. It is a control result, not an identification theorem for
observational banking data.


7.7     Partial observation is not always hidden confounding
Under randomized or recorded-history assignment, partial observation can make modeling dif-
ficult without confounding the action. History-based importance evaluation remains identified
under the sequential assumptions, although its variance may be prohibitive. A latent model
can impose structure that improves precision, with a corresponding specification risk.
  If historical staff used unrecorded information predictive of future outcomes, an accurate
P(At | Ht ) is generally insufficient. It describes selected historical actions without reconstructing

hidden information under a new policy. Tennenholtz et al. (2020); Bennett and Kallus (2023)
study this problem using specified information structures and informative proxy or bridge
conditions. Their results do not turn every fitted HMM into a causal environment.
   The empirical questions are about measurement: which private information did staff use;
which independently recorded proxies have defensible roles; could limited randomization
identify a missing transition; could a narrower policy be evaluated with existing support?
These questions can be more valuable than increasing the representation dimension.



7.7.1                      A finite bridge exposes the inverse problem

At fixed (a, x) in Equation (6.3), let Mzw = P(W = w | Z = z, A = a, X = x) and
mz = E[Y | Z = z, A = a, X = x]. A discrete bridge solves M h = m. Full column rank gives
at most one bridge in this class. A small minimum singular value lets modest noise in m
produce large changes in h. Regularization stabilizes the calculation while introducing bias.
   This explains why two predictive but almost redundant proxies may be weak for identification.
It also limits a numerical diagnostic: empirical full rank does not establish the substantive
proxy exclusions or population completeness. Sequential bridge methods additionally preserve
temporal roles and the target actor’s information. The time-independent-sampling identification
construction and proximal estimating strategy discussed in Bennett and Kallus (2023) are
distinct approaches, with different computational and regularity requirements.



7.8                  Customer behavior and the bank’s objective

A bank POMDP is not automatically a model of customer utility. Distinguish bank offer b
from household choice a. A declared dynamic logit construction has v(a, s; b) = u(a, s; b) +
βE[V (s′ ) | s, a, b] and, under centered independent Type-I extreme-value shocks of fixed scale
τ , V (s) = τ log a exp{v(a, s)/τ }. Choice probabilities are proportional to exp{v(a, s)/τ }.
                    P

Utility normalization, discounting, information and transition restrictions must be identified;
a softmax-looking policy does not supply them.
7.9. A concrete initial module                                                                           43


  Given a supported customer response law, the bank’s induced objects are

         Kb (s, s′ ) =       Pθ (a | s, b)Fθ (s′ | s, a, b),
                         X                                                X
                                                               rb (s) =       Pθ (a | s, b)m(s, b, a).
                         a                                                a

Household utility u and bank contribution m have different owners and need not be proportional.
Mortgage demand and lender behavior in Benetton (2021), and refinancing mechanisms in
Agarwal et al. (2020); Beraja et al. (2019), motivate this separation. The synthetic POMDP’s
supplied reward schedule does not estimate household utility.
   Composition therefore needs three contracts: the response module declares supported offer
interventions; finance declares ownership, discounting and terminal claims; control declares
the bank’s information and feasible actions. A fitted incumbent-choice probability alone does
not support an unmodeled marketing or pricing intervention.


7.9     A concrete initial module
The initial product should support finite states, categorical and simple parametric emissions,
observed covariates, variable trajectory lengths, explicit censoring and a declared logging-law
family. Results contain likelihood diagnostics, parameter and state uncertainty, transition
support, the observation clock and a separate causal interpretation. Prospective trajectory
views use filtering; retrospective views label smoothing.
   Small models compare EM, direct optimization and exact path enumeration. Planning
consumes an explicitly accepted environment and preserves the actor’s information. Eval-
uation fixes a policy or runs an outer training and evaluation protocol. Continuous states,
particle likelihoods and amortized inference have separate approximation and identification
work. BayesFilter can supply useful probabilistic infrastructure, but the causal action model,
intervention evidence and temporal semantics remain owned by this product. No current bank
or sibling integration is claimed.
Chapter 8

Causal discovery as constrained
scientific search

8.1    What a graph represents
A bank may want to understand whether deposit-rate changes precede withdrawals, whether a
service complaint mediates attrition, or whether an economic shock affects several products.
A discovery procedure can help organize hypotheses, but its output must state the variables,
time scale, sampling mechanism, latent-variable assumptions and edge semantics.
   A DAG specifies acyclic causal relations among variables. A CPDAG represents a Markov
equivalence class under an appropriate causally sufficient model. A PAG represents invariant
ancestral information across a class that can include hidden confounding and selection. Circle
endpoints encode uncertainty; they are not weak versions of directed arrows. Causal graphs
also differ from data-lineage graphs, whose edges represent transformations or provenance.
  Conditional independences alone often leave multiple DAGs compatible with the same
observed law (Peters et al., 2017). Temporal precedence rules out some directions, but
contemporaneous dependence, subsampling, delayed recording and hidden common causes still
matter. A graph of monthly aggregates need not preserve daily intervention semantics.

   The PC literature separates pointwise consistency from stronger high-dimensional uniform
consistency requirements (Kalisch and Bühlmann, 2007). LiNGAM and its structural-VAR
extension obtain additional directionality through non-Gaussian independent noise (Shimizu
et al., 2006; Hyvärinen et al., 2010). Granger-style prediction instead asks whether past
values improve conditional prediction. It becomes interventionally causal only with additional
structural assumptions; a common macro driver can create predictive lead-lag relations without
a direct causal effect.


8.3     Continuous optimization is a computational result
NOTEARS replaces a combinatorial DAG constraint with
                               h(W ) = tr{exp(W ◦ W )} − p = 0.                          (8.1)
For S = W ◦ W ≥ 0, each tr(S k ) sums weights of closed directed walks. Expanding the
matrix exponential shows that h(W ) = 0 precisely when no directed cycle exists (Zheng et al.,
2018). This elegant characterization makes continuous optimization possible; it does not
establish which direction is causal. DAGMA gives another smooth characterization using a log
determinant (Bello et al., 2022). Both still need a suitable structural model, regularization
and numerical checks.
   DYNOTEARS adds lagged coefficients to a structural VAR and constrains the contempo-
raneous graph (Pamfil et al., 2020). Time order already constrains lagged directions, while
identification of within-period effects depends on functional and innovation assumptions. A
group-wide monthly model that mixes accounting identities, price-setting and endogenous
demand is not automatically within those assumptions.
46                                                            Causal analysis for a universal bank


8.4     Time-series discovery and latent causes

PCMCI reduces irrelevant conditioning by estimating useful parent sets before momentary
conditional-independence tests (Runge et al., 2018). PCMCI+ adds contemporaneous links.
Its inspected assumption statement requires causal sufficiency, stationarity, sufficient maximum
lag, appropriate faithfulness and consistent tests, and excludes selection and measurement
error (Runge, 2020). Banking measurement defects therefore need explicit treatment before
applying its theorem.
   LPCMCI permits hidden common causes through temporal ancestral-graph representations
(Gerhardus and Runge, 2020). The result is a PAG with uncertainty, not a fully observed
latent-state reconstruction. Changing the lag window can change the marginal graph being rep-
resented. Store the window, conditioning tests, significance thresholds, multiplicity treatment,
background constraints and bootstrap stability with every result.
   Missing data adds another graph. Conditioning on observed records can create selection
dependencies; naive imputation can create apparently strong edges (Tu et al., 2019). A null
result can reflect weak measurements or low power, not absence of an economic mechanism.
The discovery workspace must keep measurement and missingness assumptions visible.


8.5     Continuous time, feedback and recent directions

Dynamic SCMs model variables as paths and define interventions at that level (Boeken and
Mooij, 2024). Connections between dynamical systems, interventions and equilibria require
solvability and stability assumptions (Bongers et al., 2022). Recent causal SDE results extend
Markov properties and do-calculus under specified solvability conditions (Boeken and Mooij,
2026). These are relevant to irregular transactions and continuous-rate dynamics, but do not
yet provide an automatically qualified bank estimator.
   The recent search found several useful research comparators. ITSY addresses irregular
series but explicitly assumes causal sufficiency, stationarity and MCAR (Xu et al., 2026).
LUCID routes corrections according to pervasive or local confounding signatures (Fesanghary,
2026b). The Causal-TS paper describes nonstationary temporal workflows and accelerated
independence tests (Fesanghary, 2026a). Their author-reported performance has not been
reproduced here; the most recent versions are preprints. They motivate benchmarks rather
than immediate default dependencies.
   Group-level causal background knowledge can reduce a large search problem (Ruiz de Vargas
et al., 2026). For example, an agreed temporal ordering of eligibility, assignment, receipt
and outcomes excludes implausible edges. An enterprise ontology alone supplies names and
relationships, not that causal ordering. Domain experts must justify it.


8.6     A discovery-to-study workflow

Start with a narrowly defined question and a time-respecting dataset. Record domain con-
straints, plausible omitted variables and observation mechanisms. Run transparent baseline
methods and selected challengers; compare equivalence classes, graph stability and sensitivity
to aggregation, lag windows and missingness.
   Next, choose a small set of economically meaningful candidate mechanisms. For each one,
state a proposed intervention and ask whether its effect is identified in every graph still under
consideration. If not, report a range or identify the experiment or measurement that would
8.7. A financial graph needs a unit and an intervention                                      47


distinguish models. Only then create an effect-study specification with a documented graph
choice. The change from discovered hypothesis to accepted identification assumption must be
an explicit event in the evidence record.
  This workflow can reduce wasted study design and suggest better measurement. It should
not promise to discover the bank’s unique true causal graph from all data, especially when
policies adapt and hidden information drives actions.


8.7     A financial graph needs a unit and an intervention

Consider daily balances, the posted deposit rate, customer withdrawals, funding transfers and
a market rate. “Rate causes balances” is incomplete. The rate may be an account-specific
offer, a regional posted rate or a group-average accounting yield. Balances may be end-of-day
stocks, intraday liquidity or monthly averages. A causal edge between two aggregate series
does not necessarily describe the effect of changing one customer’s offer.
   The graph specification should therefore name the unit, aggregation window, decision actor
and hypothetical intervention for every actionable node. Some nodes are accounting identities.
End balance equals beginning balance plus net flows and valuation adjustments. Treating all
terms as independent stochastic variables can create deterministic conditional relations that
violate the generic faithfulness assumptions of a discovery algorithm. The data layer should
record the identity and choose a scientifically appropriate variable representation.
   The distinction is useful even when the final graph remains uncertain. An economist
may discover that all plausible graphs leave a rate effect unidentified without a funding-cost
instrument or an experiment. That is an actionable output: obtain the missing variation or
narrow the claim. A unique-looking graph created by an arbitrary tie-breaker would be less
useful because it conceals the unresolved measurement decision.


8.8     Why observational equivalence survives unlimited data

For three variables, the DAGs X → M → Y and X ← M → Y have the same skeleton and no
unshielded collider. Both can imply X ⊥ Y | M while allowing marginal dependence. Under
ordinary observational conditional-independence assumptions, the data cannot distinguish
their causal direction. A collider X → M ← Y instead predicts marginal independence
and conditional dependence when its other assumptions hold. This is why constraint-based
discovery records equivalence information (Peters et al., 2017; Kalisch and Bühlmann, 2007).
  The economic consequences differ. In the chain, intervening on X can change Y through
M . In the common-cause graph, an intervention on X may leave Y unchanged. More
observations can estimate the common observed law more precisely without resolving that
causal ambiguity. Temporal order or an intervention can add information; a more confident
conditional-independence test alone cannot.
  A similar ambiguity occurs in the executed two-variable VAR. Its lag matrix and innovation
covariance are                           !                    !
                                   .7 0                  1 .8
                           A=              ,    Σu =            .
                                  .15 .6                .8 1

Ordering funding first gives impact column (1, .8)′ for a unit funding shock. Ordering it second
gives normalized column (1, 0)′ . Both decompositions reproduce exactly the same Gaussian
reduced-form law. Their loan responses are the second components of Ah (1, .8)′ and Ah (1, 0)′ ,
48                                                                Causal analysis for a universal bank


plotted in Figure 5.1. The impact response is 0.8 in one model and zero in the other. No
forecasting comparison can choose between them under that common law.
   Independent non-Gaussian structural innovations can break some linear equivalences under
the assumptions of LiNGAM and its time-series extension (Shimizu et al., 2006; Hyvärinen
et al., 2010). This is additional model information, not a consequence of fitting a VAR. Hidden
common causes, Gaussian innovations, misspecified lag dynamics and aggregated signals can
invalidate the argument. The discovery interface should show which restriction contributed
each orientation.


8.9       Conditional-independence testing is a statistical component
For jointly Gaussian variables, zero partial correlation corresponds to conditional independence.
One can residualize X and Y on a conditioning set S, calculate their correlation, and use an
appropriate sampling law. For nonlinear relationships, kernel, nearest-neighbor or learned
tests require different regularity and calibration. A strong nonlinear dependence can coexist
with zero ordinary correlation.
   Temporal dependence complicates the sampling distribution. A test designed for iid rows
cannot be applied blindly to overlapping lag vectors. Parent conditioning in PCMCI seeks to
remove irrelevant persistence and reduce the conditioning dimension before its final momentary
tests (Runge et al., 2018). PCMCI+ incorporates contemporaneous structure under its stated
sufficiency and stationarity restrictions (Runge, 2020). These methods improve a specified
search problem; they do not exempt the observations from their own measurement model.
   High-dimensional search also makes the testing family adaptive. With p variables and L lags,
even one test per candidate has order p2 L comparisons. Conditioning-set exploration can add
many more. An edgewise nominal level does not by itself imply graphwise error control. Any
false-discovery correction must match the tests and dependence it actually receives. Bootstrap
selection frequency is useful stability information, but it is not automatically a posterior edge
probability or a calibrated confidence level.
   The proposed benchmark therefore measures at least three objects. First, test calibration
on known independent or dependent processes under the relevant serial dependence. Second,
graph recovery under declared causal models, reporting adjacency and orientation errors
separately. Third, the downstream effect or decision loss induced by using the graph. A small
structural Hamming distance can still conceal the one orientation that reverses an important
funding decision.


8.10       Acyclic optimization and time-series structure
In a linear contemporaneous model X = XW + U , a squared-error score plus sparsity penalty
and Equation (8.1) defines an optimization problem. The acyclicity condition is exact for the
weighted adjacency matrix, but identification also depends on what distribution of U and what
score distinguish observationally equivalent parameterizations. Thresholding small coefficients
after optimization can alter the fitted distribution and the uncertainty of the selected graph.
     For lagged systems, write
                                                L
                                                X
                                 Xt = B0 Xt +         Bℓ Xt−ℓ + εt .
                                                ℓ=1

Only B0 needs a within-period acyclicity restriction in a finite unrolled time graph. Solving gives
8.11. Aggregation, missingness and changing regimes                                          49


reduced-form coefficients Aℓ = (I − B0 )−1 Bℓ and innovations ut = (I − B0 )−1 εt . Estimating
Aℓ alone therefore does not identify the structural Bℓ . DYNOTEARS fits contemporaneous
and lagged structure together under its structural model (Pamfil et al., 2020); the product
should retain both matrices rather than present reduced-form predictive coefficients as direct
mechanisms.
   Feedback can be economically real within an observation window. Rates affect flows and
flows induce repricing during the same month. Forcing an acyclic monthly contemporaneous
graph may be a convenient approximation, not a correct mechanism. Finer timing, a cyclic
structural model with well-defined solutions, or a path-level intervention can be more suitable.
Dynamic SCM and dynamical-systems work provides a language for these questions (Boeken
and Mooij, 2024; Bongers et al., 2022), while practical estimation still requires an observation
scheme and identifying restrictions.


8.11     Aggregation, missingness and changing regimes
Sampling every second period of a VAR(1) produces
                                 Xt = A2 Xt−2 + Aut−1 + ut .
Even if A is sparse, A2 can contain a nonzero (i, j) entry because of an intermediate path
j → k → i. The coarser lag graph can therefore contain an edge that represents a multi-
step mechanism. Its innovation covariance also changes. Learning the monthly graph and
interpreting each edge as a daily direct intervention would be a category error, not merely a
loss of temporal precision.
  Irregular observations add selection. An account can be measured more often after an
adverse event; staff may record a customer conversation only when assistance is considered.
Treating the resulting absence as MCAR can create or remove conditional dependencies.
Missingness-aware discovery requires assumptions about the observation process (Tu et al.,
2019). ITSY’s explicit MCAR and stationarity restrictions (Xu et al., 2026) are useful precisely
because they reveal when the method does not fit a bank’s informative observation schedule.
   A pooled graph across low-rate, crisis and high-rate regimes can also mix mechanisms.
One approach fits separate graphs in sufficiently supported regimes; another models changing
parameters or environments under declared invariance restrictions. Separate fits reduce sample
size; a shared graph can force false stability. The choice should be evaluated with temporal
holdouts and mechanism-specific diagnostics. A change-point detector locates distributional
change without establishing which causal mechanism changed or whether the cause was policy.
  Recent LUCID and Causal-TS proposals address important confounding or nonstationarity
challenges (Fesanghary, 2026b,a). They should be included as research comparators on
banking-specific synthetic mechanisms and carefully bounded real studies. Their newness and
author-reported performance do not establish that they solve aggregation, hidden logging or
measurement selection simultaneously.


8.12     From graph uncertainty to a useful answer
Suppose a discovery method returns a set of compatible graphs G. For each G, let ΘG be
                                                            S
the compatible effect set under its assumptions. The union G∈G ΘG describes what remains
compatible when graph uncertainty is retained. If a candidate policy is economically preferable
across that set, the decision can be robust even without unique orientation. If the set spans
both a gain and a loss, reporting one graph’s point effect would hide a material uncertainty.
50                                                            Causal analysis for a universal bank


   The representation must distinguish an equivalence class justified by theory from a convenient
collection of bootstrap graphs. The latter is a stability sample and need not contain every
compatible graph. Likewise, a PAG endpoint carries ancestral information under a latent-
variable model; replacing a circle by an arrow because its score is slightly larger changes the
identification claim.
  A research workbench can then rank additional observations or interventions by their
potential to resolve the consequential ambiguity. For example, randomized rate offers in a
supported population may distinguish a rate-response edge, while an independent liquidity
measurement may help separate demand from funding pressure. The first release can present
these as analyst-authored study proposals tied to graph alternatives. Automatic optimal
experiment selection would require a model of information value and operating constraints
and is a separate research feature.


8.13     The discovery module’s construction contract
Inputs include variable definitions, population, observation clock, aggregation, lag window,
background constraints, hidden-variable and selection assumptions, conditional-independence
test and multiplicity policy. Outputs include graph type, endpoint marks, edge evidence,
unresolved alternatives, stability information and sensitivity to timing and missingness. Every
display of a causal effect identifies the graph and additional assumptions used to compute it.
   The product should initially wrap established temporal and latent-aware algorithms, retain
their native diagnostics and compare simple structural baselines. It should use domain
groupings to reduce search only when those groupings supply justified background restrictions
(Ruiz de Vargas et al., 2026). Data-lineage links, semantic similarity and causal arrows remain
different edge types. Their integration in one interface is useful only if their meanings remain
explicit.
            Part III

Banking studies from decision to
             value




               51
Chapter 9

A deposit-policy study from rollout
to funding value

9.1     The owner’s decision and the financial account

Suppose the group funding committee is considering a temporary savings-rate enhancement.
The retail business expects retained deposits; treasury values the funding; finance pays interest
on qualifying balances; and the customer receives a higher rate. The relevant bank decision is
whether the incremental funding value exceeds the incremental interest and operating costs
over a specified horizon. An effect on account balances is one input to that decision, not its
answer.
   The committee needs three quantities kept separate: balances in the promoted product,
total external funding retained by the group, and incremental economic contribution. An
internal transfer from another group account can increase the first with little change in the
second. Paying a higher rate on incumbent balances can make the third negative even when
both balance measures rise. This decomposition should be visible in the first report.
   The empirical literature suggests mechanisms and designs. The deposits channel in Drechsler
et al. (2017) connects monetary policy, local deposit market power, funding flows and lending.
Its within-bank branch comparison uses geographic concentration while controlling bank-
specific opportunities; its interpretation relies on banks being able to move funding between
branches. The paper’s subsequent lending comparisons operate at different aggregation levels.
It does not supply the effect of a new bank’s account- level retention offer. The product should
make that distinction explicit when an analyst imports a mechanism from a published study.



9.2     The data contract before estimation

The proposed bank implementation begins with a fixed eligible cohort before announcement. It
preserves branch and household identity as of that date, the original assignment, the announced
terms, delivery, take-up and later closure. It then reconstructs daily balances, interest, external
flows and internal transfer links under a stated accounting cutoff. A corrected transaction
changes a later readout while leaving the original information set and assignment intact.
   Households moving between branches require a declared attribution rule. Freezing baseline
assignment preserves an intention-to-treat interpretation; following current branch membership
can select on the policy response. Cross-branch displacement also challenges untreated donors.
A group-wide study can use household-level outcomes while clustering by randomized or rollout

9.3      A complete synthetic rollout

The executed study observes 96 branches for 30 months. Twenty-four branches adopt in each
of months 12, 18 and 24, with 24 never adopting. Months are indexed from zero. Cohort labels
are fixed and branch disturbances are independent of them. Untreated balances, in millions of
dollars, are

                Bit (0) = 30 + αi + 0.07t + 0.4 sin(t/3) + ϵit ,                               (9.1)
                                2                                                   2
                    αi ∼ N (0, 3 ),      ϵit = 0.65ϵi,t−1 + ηit ,   ηit ∼ N (0, 0.28 ),        (9.2)

with the first disturbance drawn at the innovation scale. For cohort g and event month
k = t − g ≥ 0, the balance effect is

                            τgk = {0.85 + 0.025(g − 12)}(1 + 0.14k).

This law imposes untreated parallel trends while allowing heterogeneous, growing effects. It
is designed to compare targets and estimators rather than simulate every feature of deposit
demand.
   For every supported (g, t), estimate the change from g − 1 among that cohort minus the same
change among never-treated branches. Average all treated cohort-month cells equally. Because
all cohorts have 24 branches, this equals an equal-weight average over treated branch-months.
It gives early cohorts more total weight because they contribute more treated months. A bank
wanting an equal-cohort or balanced-event-window target would use different declared weights.
  The challenger fits a single treatment indicator with branch and month effects. It estimates
a different weighted combination when effects evolve with adoption time, as explained in
Chapter 3. The study also calculates a known reference by comparing the generated potential
outcomes for the same branch-months. Those potential outcomes are available only to the
synthetic evaluator.

and USD 1,800 monthly program cost per treated branch. Under the stipulated monthly

9.5       Fitted results and uncertainty
The same cohort-time estimator is applied separately to balances and observed contribution.
Whole branches are resampled within each adoption cohort in 499 bootstrap samples, retaining
each trajectory and the fixed cohort counts. The percentile intervals condition on this rollout
design and the supplied common macro path. They are not a repeated-sample coverage
qualification for a bank rollout.

           Outcome                True effect Cohort ATT             95% interval    TWFE
           Balances (USD m)            1.780        1.689          [1.564, 1.816]    1.442

Table 9.2: One fixed synthetic rollout. The reference is the realized finite-population potential-

   The contribution estimate is approximately USD −5, 219 per treated branch-month, with
interval [−5, 498, −4, 936]. Under the stipulated design and account, the rollout loses money
despite retaining balances. The appropriate decision is to reject this broad offer or investigate
a different, explicitly evaluated policy. Selecting a more favorable balance estimator would not
remove the cost of repricing incumbent funds.
  The balance and contribution estimates share outcomes and branches. For a portfolio of
more detailed cash components, the implementation retains their joint bootstrap or influence
contributions. It should not form a purported interval for total contribution by adding
separately calculated marginal endpoints. The simple account here allows contribution to be
observed directly, avoiding an unnecessary two-stage uncertainty approximation.
